newsitem.title: USA: Growth, tough policies give economic hope to Africa.
newsitem.headline: Growth, tough policies give economic hope to Africa.

text.p: The countries of sub-Saharan Africa are still bit players in the global game of capital flows characterising the world's emerging markets.

But economic growth across the continent and the willingness of many states to swallow the tough monetarist medicine of the International Monetary Fund has provided a glimmer of hope for investors and for the poor.

"As long as African governments are prepared to implement prudent macro-economic policies with open markets, both domestically and externally,and with exchange rates that reflect the real state of their economies, Africa can increase growth rates to about 10 percent a year," said Emmannuel Tumusiime-Mutebile, secretary to the Ugandan Treasury.
"If countries can sustain that growth for 25 or 30 years, I have no doubt that mass poverty can be eliminated."

Uganda, which launched an IMF-backed reform programme four years ago, is viewed as one of Africa's economic success stories, with one-time three-digit annual inflation now less than 10 percent, a stable currency and steady economic growth.

But the economies of countries in the region remain fragile and vulnerable to events outside a government's control -- droughts, fluctuating commodity prices or political unrest outside their borders.

Structural reform tends to lag monetary and fiscal change and few countries have moved on to what the IMF describes as "second-generation reforms", creating a level playing field for investment by ensuring the legal system works, the infrastructure is in place and corruption is kept low.

"There is progress, but it is very fragile," said Evangelos Calamitsis, responsible for 48 countries as the director of the IMF's Africa department. He described capital flows to African countries as "dismal".

"Growth averaging 6.5 percent a year is not enough if the population is growing three percent ... Given the fact that there was what they called the lost decade of the 80s, there is a lot of catching up to do."

The IMF has support programmes with 21 of Calamitsis's 48 countries and a delegation is travelling to the Democratic Republic of the Congo -- formerly Zaire -- next week for its first talks with the administration there.

"I hope that the new Zaire -- I'll call it that to avoid confusion with the other Congo -- will look at the experience of Uganda and see what lessons it can draw from that experience," said Calamitsis.
"The new Zaire has had a lot of problems in the past, but it is obvious that they have to bring inflation under control, restore financial discipline and stamp out corruption."
Calamitsis said priorities across Africa would focus on second generation reform.
"Many African countries have done well on the macro side or have tried to put their house in order there," he said. "What they have not done, or not done enough, is the so-called structural reforms."
Tumusiime-Mutebile said growth had to be accompanied by what he described as human capital development -- ensuring access to water, health care and education.

"Economic growth must be broadly-based economic growth, it must be growth which is intensive in the use of assets which the poor have, it must be growth that puts money in the pockets of the poor and it must be growth that is accompanied by human capital development," he said.
